issues.legal_issue: A redemption suit may proceed against a surviving mortgagee when it has abated against another mortgagee, if the claimant offers to pay the entire mortgage debt to the surviving mortgagee and abandons relief against the absent mortgagee.
material_facts: The mortgaged property had been divided between two assignees of the mortgagee’s rights, one holding rights in the houses and the other in a common latrine.
The second mortgagee died during the appeal, and his heirs were not brought on the record, so the appeal abated against him.
The claimant offered to pay the entire mortgage amount to the surviving mortgagee and disclaimed any relief against the property held by the absent mortgagee.
The absent mortgagee had not contested the suit.
issues.conclusion: The suit could proceed against the surviving mortgagee despite abatement against the other mortgagee, provided the claimant paid the entire mortgage consideration and gave up the claim against the absent mortgagee.
issues.legal_principle: Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act prevents a person interested only in a share of mortgaged property from redeeming only that share by paying a proportionate part of the debt, preserving the integrity of the mortgage. Order XXXIV, Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure addresses parties to mortgage suits. However, where the claimant pays the entire debt to the mortgagees before the court and gives up rights against those not before it, redemption may be decreed against the mortgagees who are present. The Court relied on Motilal Yadav v. Samal Bechar (1930) 54 Bom. 625 and held that a party necessary to the suit need not necessarily be necessary to the appeal.

predicates.redemption_suit: The proceeding seeks redemption of property subject to a mortgage.
predicates.co_mortgagee_died_without_successors_bei: One of the mortgagees died and that mortgagee’s successors were not brought into the proceeding.
predicates.claimant_offers_entire_mortgage_debt_to_: The claimant offers to pay the whole mortgage debt to the mortgagee who remains in the proceeding.
predicates.claimant_abandons_claim_against_absent_m: The claimant gives up any relief against the mortgagee who is not before the court.
predicates.redemption_may_proceed_against_surviving: The redemption proceeding may continue against the mortgagee who remains before the court.

issues.definition: When a redemption proceeding concerns multiple mortgagees, one mortgagee’s absence following death does not prevent redemption against a surviving mortgagee if the claimant offers the entire debt and gives up claims against the absent mortgagee.

issues.legal_issue: Statements disclaiming a person’s interest in mortgaged property do not estop that person or a successor from asserting the right to redeem unless the requirements for estoppel are established.
material_facts: Notices from the mortgagee’s side called on the mortgagor’s heirs to undertake repairs or redeem the property and to meet repair expenses.
The mortgagor’s son, widow, and daughter responded in terms indicating that they had no concern with, or responsibility for, the property or the relevant dealings.
The mortgagee-side purchaser claimed that he would not have acquired the mortgagee’s rights had those statements not been made.
The statements were not made to the purchaser claiming estoppel, concerned the heirs’ rights rather than a fact, and did not establish that the purchaser changed his position because of them.
The purchaser or his predecessor knew, or could have learned, the true position concerning the rights in the property.
issues.conclusion: The statements amounted at most to admissions, not estoppel, and the requirements of Section 115 of the Evidence Act were not satisfied.
issues.legal_principle: Section 115 of the Evidence Act requires a representation by a person or authorised agent to another, concerning an existing fact, intended to be relied on and believed, which actually and proximately induces prejudicial action by the person claiming estoppel, who must not know the true state of affairs; only the person to whom the representation was made or for whom it was designed may rely on it. Admissions are evidence but are not conclusive and may be explained or withdrawn, whereas estoppel creates a bar. Estoppel concerns facts, not rights, and there can be no estoppel against a statute. No earlier case is cited on this issue.

rule.if: estoppel_claim_in_redemption_suit and (representation_not_made_to_claimant or representation_concerns_right_not_fact or no_induced_prejudicial_change or claimant_knew_or_could_learn_true_position)

predicates.estoppel_claim_in_redemption_suit: A party claims that another person’s statement or conduct bars the assertion of a right in a redemption proceeding.
predicates.representation_not_made_to_claimant: The person claiming estoppel was not the recipient of the representation and was not someone for whom it was designed.
predicates.representation_concerns_right_not_fact: The representation concerned a legal right rather than the existence of a fact.
predicates.no_induced_prejudicial_change: The representation did not actually induce the claimant to change position to the claimant’s prejudice.
predicates.claimant_knew_or_could_learn_true_positi: The claimant knew, or had the means to learn, the true state of affairs.
predicates.estoppel_not_established: The claimed representation does not create an estoppel barring the assertion of the right.

issues.definition: In a redemption proceeding, estoppel is not established if the claimant did not receive a factual representation, was not induced to change position prejudicially, or knew or could learn the true position.
